Insurance company has also raised a defence that the victim contributed to the accident in as much as it has been admitted by PW1 that the victim held a valid driving licence but never produced it.
It has been pleaded that in absence of a driving licence, petitioners are liable to deduction in compensation on account of contributory negligence.

In the considered opinion of this Tribunal the plea of contributory negligence is unsustainable in the present circumstances even if the victim is assumed to have been driving the motorcycle without a valid driving licence.

It has been repeatedly affirmed in numerous judicial pronouncement that in order to hold contributory negligence upon the victim of an accident, it must be demonstrated by the insurance company that the act of the victim directly contributed to the occurrence of the accident or exacerbated its impact.

A mere traffic violation may not always contribute to an accident and unless insurance company produces some independent evidence to show that the injured did not know how to drive or committed an act which contributed or would have attributed to his lack of skills of driving a motorcycle.
In the instant case, insurance company has not even taken a plea that the victim was driving on the wrong side or in a manner which contributed to the collision.
Hence, no contributory negligence on the part of the victim is proved.

15. In totality of circumstances, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the petitioner been able to prove on the scales of preponderance of probabilities that the accident in question, took place due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by its driver/respondent no.1 on the date and time of accident.

In the considered opinion of this Tribunal the plea of contributory negligence is unsustainable in the present circumstances even if the victim is assumed to have been driving the motorcycle without a valid driving licence.
It has been repeatedly affirmed in numerous judicial pronouncement that in order to hold contributory negligence upon the victim of an accident, it must be demonstrated by the insurance company that the act of the victim directly contributed to the occurrence of the accident or exacerbated its impact.
A mere traffic violation may not always contribute to an accident and unless insurance company produces some independent evidence to show that the injured did not know how to drive or committed an act which contributed or would have attributed to his lack of skills of driving a motorcycle.
In the instant case, insurance company has not even taken a plea that the victim was driving on the wrong side or in a manner which contributed to the collision.
Hence, no contributory negligence on the part of the victim is proved.
As such, all the petitioners must have been dependent on the deceased and accordingly entitled to compensation under the head of dependency.
